analysis.one_liner: Requires the Labor Department to issue a new federal ergonomics standard to prevent workplace repetitive-stress injuries.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to restore a workplace ergonomics rule won favorable committee action but never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After Congress repealed a Clinton-era ergonomics rule in 2001, this bill would have ordered the Labor Department to write a new rule within two years requiring employers to address workplace ergonomic hazards — the repetitive lifting, bending, and reaching that cause back and limb injuries. It covered every industry where such hazards exist and feasible fixes are available, and it required prevention efforts before injuries happen. The bill cleared the Senate labor committee but never came up for a vote in the full Senate or the House.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 1,000,000 workers a year who lose work time because of job-related musculoskeletal disorders, and employers who bear part of the $45-$54 billion annual cost of those injuries in compensation, lost wages, and lost productivity [S3]. Workers in nursing homes, warehouses, meatpacking, and other physically demanding jobs would have gained the most, since employers would have been required to redesign hazardous tasks before workers got hurt [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers with repetitive-stress and back injuries

how_it_helps.text: The bill directed the Secretary of Labor to issue a final ergonomics rule within two years of enactment, taking effect within 90 days after it was issued, so the standard could not sit indefinitely without action [S2] [S3].

The rule would have had to address work-related musculoskeletal disorders and cover all industries where workers face ergonomic hazards and there are economically and technologically feasible ways to control them [S3].
The bill emphasized prevention before injuries occur and required the Labor Department to prepare training and compliance materials for both employers and employees [S3].

The bill's findings cite a National Academy of Sciences report calling work-related musculoskeletal disorders an important national health problem, with about a million workers a year losing work time and $45-$54 billion in annual costs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would have had to identify ergonomic hazards and change work practices, equipment, or job design to meet the standard. Those costs would fall heaviest on labor-intensive industries like nursing homes, food processing, warehousing, and manufacturing, and some portion would likely pass through to consumers in prices [S3]. The bill required the rule to account for the cost and feasibility of compliance, which would temper but not eliminate these expenses [S3].

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs: employers would bear real expenses to redesign jobs and equipment, and the bill itself acknowledged the rule must take 'the cost and feasibility of compliance' into account — an honest supporter concedes this is a mandatory cost on businesses, with no automatic federal funding to help small firms comply [S3].

Design risk: the bill ordered a new rule rather than writing the safety requirements itself, leaving the details — and their cost — to the Labor Department's discretion. Opponents of the repealed 2000 rule had argued a broad ergonomics standard could saddle employers with requirements that outpaced the evidence for any given workplace, a concern the bill tried to address by basing the standard on the National Academy of Sciences report and proven employer practices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a large, well-documented problem: about a million workers a year lose time from work with back and limb injuries, at $45-$54 billion annually in compensation, lost wages, and lost productivity [S3]. The tradeoff is mandatory compliance spending by employers, with the burden concentrated in physically demanding industries. The bill tried to narrow the cost side — requiring feasibility analysis, proven industry practices, and no expansion of state workers' compensation [S3] — but a rule of this breadth would still have imposed significant costs on some employers. Weighing a million lost-work injuries a year against those costs, the public health case was strong, though the exact burden depended on rule details never written because the bill died.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate labor committee approved the bill favorably in June 2002, but it never came up for a vote in the full Senate or the House before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Breaux introduced the bill on April 17, 2002, with 27 original senators joining; it was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S3] [S5].
Thirty-seven senators eventually cosponsored the bill — 35 of the 49 Senate Democrats, 1 of the 49 Senate Republicans, and 1 of the 2 independents [S4].
On June 19, 2002, the committee ordered the bill to be reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, meaning it was rewritten but endorsed [S5].
No further action was taken: the bill never reached the Senate floor for a vote, and the House never took it up. The 107th Congress ended January 3, 2003, and the bill died [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced new ergonomics compliance obligations came out ahead, since the bill died without a vote. Workers with job-related repetitive-stress injuries are left without a federal ergonomics standard, as the 2000 rule remains repealed.

for.name: Sen. John Breaux
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing the Labor Department to reissue an ergonomics rule, and recruited 26 original cosponsors

for.name: 35 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making up all but two of its 37 cosponsors

for.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Referred the bill and on June 19, 2002 ordered it reported favorably with a substitute amendment

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor, the only Senate Republican to back the bill besides its later cosponsors

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and employer coalitions
against.role: Business groups that had opposed and helped repeal the 2000 ergonomics rule
against.what_they_did: Opposed revival of a federal ergonomics standard after backing its repeal in 2001

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily but not entirely Democratic: 35 of 49 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 independents cosponsored, joined by just 1 of 49 Senate Republicans, and the bill was never voted on in either chamber.

industries.industry: Employers in labor-intensive industries (nursing homes, warehousing, food processing, manufacturing)
industries.note: A federal ergonomics standard would have required these employers to identify hazardous tasks and redesign them, imposing compliance costs concentrated in industries with heavy lifting and repetitive motion. Their interest in avoiding the rule ran against workers' interest in injury prevention, though some employers also lose from the injuries themselves through compensation and lost productivity [S3].

industries.industry: Occupational safety and health consulting and compliance services
industries.note: The bill required the Labor Department to develop training materials and outreach, and a new standard would have created demand for workplace ergonomics assessment and compliance help [S3].
